name: Merger-Arb Deal-Break Protective Put
aliases: downside insurance on an arb position
summary: Buy an out-of-the-money put on an announced acquisition target to cap the loss if the deal collapses - the arbitrageur's insurance leg, converting an open-ended binary risk into a known cost.

legs.strike_rule: 100 shares of an announced target, held as the arbitrage position
strike at or slightly above the estimated undisturbed (pre-announcement) price - this is the price the stock reverts to on a break, not a delta-selected strike
legs.dte_rule: expiry at or beyond the expected close date, 60-180 DTE

max_profit: (deal price - basis - put premium) x 100 - the deal spread, less the cost of insurance
max_loss: (basis - put strike + put premium) x 100 - defined, and that definition is the entire purpose of the leg

greeks.delta: +100 from the shares less the put's delta, typically +80 to +95 per unit
greeks.gamma: positive, and the only convexity in an otherwise linear arb position
greeks.theta: negative - the premium is a running insurance cost against the deal spread
greeks.vega: positive, which matters because deal-stock IV spikes on the first hint of trouble

typical_dte: 60-180 DTE, sized to outlast the expected close
when_to_use: Any merger-arb position where the deal spread is thin and the break gap is large - which is most of them. The bank has speculative takeover call buying but nothing that hedges an arb book, and this is the leg that makes the arb survivable.
entry_rules: Only on announced deals with a definitive agreement; the undisturbed price must be observable from the pre-announcement chart.
Strike selection is fundamental, not delta-based: strike >= the 20-day VWAP ending the day before the announcement. Delta will typically be 0.05-0.15 and that is expected.
Put premium <= 40% of the gross deal spread ((deal price - basis) x 100). If insurance costs more than 40% of the return, the arb is not worth doing.
Expiry at or beyond the expected close date plus 30 days, to survive a routine timeline slip.
Long put only. Never finance it by selling a put below (that reintroduces exactly the break risk being hedged) and never by selling a call below the deal price.
OI >= 100 at the chosen strike; if no listed strike sits near the undisturbed price, the deal cannot be hedged this way - size the position down instead.
Position size <= 5% of equity per deal even when hedged.
management_rules: Hold the put to the deal close; it is insurance, not a trade, and selling it because it has lost value is selling the hedge at exactly the wrong time.
Roll the put out if the close date slips beyond its expiry, paying the additional premium out of the deal spread.
If the put's value doubles on deal-risk news, do NOT monetize it while the shares are still held - that is the moment it is needed.
Reassess the whole position, shares and put together, on any regulatory challenge; the correct response is usually to exit both, not to trade the hedge.
exit_rules: On a completed deal: the put expires worthless or is sold for scrap; close it rather than leaving a stub position on a delisting security.

On a deal break: sell the shares and the put in the same session; the put will be deep ITM and must be SOLD, never exercised, unless the market is too wide to trade - exercising is acceptable here only because the shares are held, and it must be logged as an incident response.
Close all legs before the underlying's delisting date in a cash-out close.
Never hold a long put on a security after its shares have been cashed out.
assignment_risk: None - the only option leg is long. The stock-delivery path is exercising the long put, which is a deliberate act against shares already held, and is the intended response only in a broken-deal scenario with an untradeable option market.
buying_power: Shares plus the put's debit; no short-option requirement.
liquidity_needs: Far-OTM puts on deal stocks are among the thinnest options listed - expect wide markets and treat the quoted premium as the real cost, not the mid.
common_mistakes: Choosing the strike by delta instead of by the undisturbed price; financing the put by selling something (which reinstates the risk); monetizing the hedge on the first scare; letting the put expire before the deal actually closes.
family: Completeness gap-fill (cross-family): ratio/naked-financed put and call structures, quantity-unbalanced condors and strangles, stock+option overlays and monetizations, capital-protection and hybrid builds, 0DTE four-leg income, volatility-surface and relative-value trades, event-driven overlays, and roll/adjustment structures
